articles.title: ‘Seattle’s answer to YC Demo Day’: 25 startups pitch investors from across the country at AI House
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: AI House brought investors from as far as Boston, New York, Colorado and the Bay Area to Seattle this week for something the city’s startup scene has rarely tried: a demo day meant to help bring outside money to local founders.

Twenty-five early-stage startups pitched at the event, held Wednesday at the startup incubator and venture capital fund’s offices on Pier 70. Many of them weren’t part of AI House’s own portfolio, and that was by design, said Yifan Zhang , an AI House managing director, who came up with the idea for the event.

“We all complained about not having enough capital here, but no one was doing anything about it,” Zhang said. So AI House tapped its own connections to investors in other parts of the country, she said, and “people flew in from all over for this.”

Investors in attendance included Mike Vernal , a partner at San Francisco-based Conviction; Emily Melton , founder and managing partner of Threshold Ventures; and Rob Go , co-founder of Boston-based NextView Ventures. Many well-known Seattle-based venture capitalists also attended the event.
Zhang said she wanted the lineup to show multiple sides of Seattle: startups built around real problems and revenue, and technologists doing “crazy ambitious things.”
Theo Ellis , CEO of Seattle mortgage-tech startup Friday Harbor , called it “Seattle’s answer to YC Demo Day,” a reference to Y Combinator’s showcase in the Bay Area.

Many of the city’s startups are “not necessarily in the flashiest spaces,” he said, but they have real customers and are growing fast. For his part, Ellis said, mortgage lending technology is “not exactly nuclear-powered robots landing on Jupiter, but it’s an enormous market with a lot of businesses willing to pay for it.”
Ellis told the crowd during his pitch that Friday Harbor underwrote 0.6% of all U.S. residential mortgage applications in August, and that the company is starting to raise its Series A round.

Many of the companies that pitched have been covered by GeekWire. In addition to Friday Harbor , they included Optimly , Vantari , Jinn Labs , GateIn , Casium , Orbital Robotics , Viata , Ridge AI , Caddi , Lev , Aria (formerly Alpyne Labs) and Synthesize Bio .
Others were new to us, at least in their current incarnations:

Closing the event, Jacob Colker, AI House co-founder and managing director, made his pitch to the out-of-town investors, building on the themes in his recent GeekWire guest column and a rallying cry he delivered during Seattle Tech Week in July.

The region is full of “space, science, tech, bio, health, startup builders,” he said, with far more good ideas than local investors can fund. “The reality is there’s just not enough capital in the Pacific Northwest.” That’s where the visitors come in, he said, predicting that they’ll find “great investment opportunities and great deals.”
Seattle, Colker said, “is worth your time, your investment, your focus, your energy.”

articles.title: Tech vet takes a fresh swing at the country club with a golf and social hub in old Seattle industrial space
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Inside a sprawling former industrial building just a chip shot from the Lake Washington Ship Canal, a Seattle tech veteran and his longtime friend are building the kind of golf and social sanctuary that they feel modern Seattle is missing.

Founded by tech veteran Shankar Sundaram , a former Boeing engineer and enterprise sales leader, alongside co-founder Ryan Schaffer , a University of Washington grad who also worked at Boeing, East West Club aims to reimagine the traditional country club.

Inspired by the multi-generational Indian household Sundaram grew up in as well as the close-knit neighborhood clubs of his East Coast youth, the name East West is a nod to bridging those traditional cultural values of family, community, and hospitality with a modern Pacific Northwest lifestyle.
The ultimate goal is to create a “third place” centered around genuine, family-friendly connection rather than corporate networking or status.

“A lot of the clubs in Seattle are a little bit older and maybe just built for a different time, for a different demographic, and we’ve changed,” Sundaram told GeekWire during a tour of the space this week at 10 Dravus St. in the Queen Anne neighborhood. “We don’t have six hours to go spend at a country club. We also don’t have $100,000 to go join.”
The vision for East West Club is starting to take shape across multiple indoor and outdoor spaces in what used to be a metal fabrication studio run by the late artist David Gulassa .

Spread across nearly 8,000 square feet between two buildings, the space retains its industrial roots with exposed timber beams, rich wood accents, and high concrete walls. Heavy construction on the primary building hasn’t started yet as the team awaits final permits from the city, but once built out, the footprint will feature a “golf lab” with wide indoor simulator bays and 500 square feet of digital putting space, alongside a private 19-foot immersive simulator bay.
The broader plan includes a quiet library lounge, a pour-your-own-beer wall, a café area, and a back-alley wellness nook featuring dry saunas and red-light therapy.

Sundaram, who is married to Armoire founder and CEO Ambika Singh , wants the club to serve as a convenient, family-friendly extension of members’ homes — a place where people can drop in for an hour rather than committing an entire day.
“We want you to bring as many people as you want,” Sundaram said. “We want you to host meetings here. We want you to actually come here and do your work here.”
East West Club will also function as an events space, where members can come together for curated gatherings, tastings, music, workshops, speaker events and more.

Rather than building out a full commercial restaurant, the club plans to rely heavily on local neighborhood partnerships. Sundaram is leaning on friends for advice on the café and coffee setup and talking to neighborhood spots about possible daily fare, alongside monthly curated dinners hosted by guest chefs.

“A big part of the vision for East West is to use the club as a platform to bring together some of the best of Seattle — partnering with great local restaurants, chefs, wineries, breweries, golf and fitness professionals, and other people doing interesting things around the city,” Sundaram said. “We want the experience to constantly evolve and give members new reasons to come together.”

To fund the buildout, Sundaram and Schaffer are opting for a community-driven bootstrap model rather than taking on heavy debt or institutional equity . They are capping their initial “founder” cohort at 100 members, asking early adopters to buy in upfront .

For the first tier of 25 founding members, a $25,000 buy-in covers four years of all-inclusive family membership, along with a $450 quarterly food and beverage credit. The early bet appears to be paying off: after launching a simple waitlist on LinkedIn three months ago that drew 120 sign-ups, Sundaram invited an initial batch of 14 people to tour the unfinished space three weeks ago — and 13 of them committed on the spot.

“These early folks are taking the biggest risk,” Sundaram said . “Prepaying for something is not very common… but we’re funding this through getting 75 to 100 founders . The total club capacity is 250 people, so the idea is, if every founder goes and gets two people, that’s the club .”
Subsequent founder tiers will gradually increase in price, and once the club opens its doors — targeted for March 2027 — the model will shift to standard initiation fees and monthly dues.

Members won’t have to wait until 2027 to start gathering, either. The team plans to open a temporary “Founders Clubhouse” to early members by the end of September, kicking off a full calendar of social programming, tastings, and events throughout October — including an Oct. 11 open house — while construction proceeds on the other spaces.
If the Queen Anne location reaches its 250-member capacity, Sundaram and Schaffer already have eyes on scaling the concept, perhaps with an Eastside location.

While indoor simulator technology is a core anchor of the space, Sundaram noted that golf is not the sole prerequisite for joining. Roughly half of the initial 14 founding members who signed up do not even play golf, seeing value instead in having a neighborhood spot to host friends, throw parties, or watch sports.

For those who do want to hit the virtual links, the club plans to partner with local instructors for lessons and youth programs, but the broader design caters as much to casual socializing as it does to perfecting a swing.

When asked about competition, Sundaram points out that East West Club isn’t trying to compete with commercial entertainment chains like Five Iron Golf or high-end, pure-play golf training centers like Evergreen Golf Club.

“If you just want to go hit up a sim and go have a burger and fries, there’s lots of spaces for that,” Sundaram said. “In the city, there’s nothing that’s like this. Golf is the glue, but nobody else is really bringing in this modern aesthetic.”

articles.title: Tech Moves: Microsoft AI exec joins Niantic Spatial; Allen fund names first investment chief; Zillow AI leader heads to Stripe
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: — Niantic Spatial hired Dave Citron as chief product officer. He joined from Microsoft AI, where he was corporate vice president of product on the Superintelligence team and helped build and launch Microsoft’s first frontier foundation models.

San Francisco-based Niantic Spatial, spun out of Pokémon Go maker Niantic , builds spatial AI models and services, including a visual positioning system trained in part on images crowdsourced from Pokémon Go players. The company has an engineering team in Bellevue, Wash.

The Seattle-area executive was previously senior director of product for the Gemini app at Google DeepMind and worked on Google Meet and Google Duo. He began his career at Microsoft in 2005, helping take OneDrive from its first release to more than 200 million monthly users.
“AI is remarkably good at reading and writing, but it still doesn’t understand the physical world well enough to act in it safely,” Citron said in the announcement.

— The Fund for Science and Technology , the Seattle-based foundation responsible for giving away a large portion of the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen’s fortune, named Jane Dietze its first chief investment officer. She starts Jan. 4, 2027, after finishing the year at Brown University, where she has held that role since 2018.

Brown says its endowment grew from $3.2 billion to $8 billion over the 10 years through fiscal 2025. Her deputy, Joshua Kennedy, will succeed her. Dietze previously held investment roles at Bowdoin College, Fortress Investment Group and Columbia Capital.

The foundation launched publicly in August 2025 with a mandate to deploy at least $500 million over four years in bioscience, the environment and AI for good. It also funds the Allen Institute and Ai2 , the Allen Institute for AI.

The fund started with a $3.1 billion endowment from Allen’s estate and is expected to oversee a large portion of the proceeds from the sale of Allen’s sports teams. Its first CEO, Lynda Stuart, stepped down in May .

— Nicholas Stevens joined payments giant Stripe as head of product for agentic commerce, working from Seattle, after a decade at Zillow . He was most recently Zillow’s vice president of product for AI and data, leading product strategy for the company’s AI products and data platform.
His LinkedIn profile notes that he drove the partnership that made Zillow one of seven global launch partners for OpenAI’s ChatGPT apps platform. He previously worked in product at Prismatic.
“I believe AI buying & selling on your behalf can be magical,” he wrote.

— Scowtt , a Kirkland, Wash.-based startup that uses AI to predict which sales prospects will become customers, named Ben Trenda chief revenue officer. Trenda is an ad tech veteran who worked at Overture/Yahoo, AOL and Rubicon Project, and co-founded iSocket. Scowtt says it is approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue.

— The American Astronomical Society named University of Washington astronomy professor Emily Levesque the next editor in chief of its journals, including The Astrophysical Journal. She takes charge in August 2027, succeeding Ethan Vishniac.

— ThriftBooks , the online used-book seller founded in Seattle in 2003, named Carla Anderson Skogland chief financial officer. She had been interim CFO since April. Anderson Skogland, who is based in the Seattle area, was previously CFO of Sono Bello. She spent 11 years at Amazon, and earlier worked at T-Mobile and for more than 15 years at Starbucks.

— Michael Mann is stepping down as executive director of Clean & Prosperous , a climate policy group that backed Washington’s Climate Commitment Act, once a successor is chosen. He took over on an interim basis from the late founder David Giuliani and led the group for five years. Mann, founder of consulting firm Cyan Strategies, previously led the City of Seattle’s Office of Sustainability and Environment.

— Lani Ramos joined Yoodli , a Seattle startup that uses AI roleplays for communications training, to build its renewals function. Ramos spent 13 years at Tableau and Salesforce, most recently as director of renewal for North America.

— Former Starbucks CFO Rachel Ruggeri joined the board of San Diego-based Jack in the Box . Ruggeri, a Seattle-area finance leader, spent more than two decades at Starbucks and was its CFO from 2021 to March 2025. She also serves on the board of Stryker.

— Victor Fetter is stepping down at the end of the year as chief technology and business systems officer at Everett, Wash.-based Fortive after nearly seven years. Rich Noonan , Fortive’s chief information security and technology operations officer, will become CIO. Fetter, who is based in Mississippi, plans to expand his board work and angel investing.

articles.title: Microsoft unveils all-in-one Copilot app, taking on Anthropic and OpenAI in new push to boost adoption
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft on Friday morning unveiled its long-promised Copilot “super app” — without officially calling it that — combining AI chat, coding and long-running agents into a unified app for business and personal use.

The new version of the Copilot app adds sections called Home, which combines chat with Microsoft’s Cowork agent ; Code, which lets people build their own apps and tools by describing them; and Autopilot, where people can set up their own always-on AI agents.
It also brings full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot, so people can create and edit documents with AI and their co-workers without switching apps.

The announcement is Microsoft’s answer to OpenAI and Anthropic, which have been combining chat, coding and agents in their own apps and selling them directly to businesses that have long been Microsoft’s core customers. Microsoft also uses models from both companies in Copilot, alongside its own.

Partners and rivals: Microsoft executives contrasted the company’s approach with OpenAI and Anthropic during an event Wednesday, according to a transcript provided by Microsoft. The pitch is aimed at corporate IT departments, which have long relied on Microsoft for security and compliance.

Jacob Andreou, the executive vice president who leads Copilot , said Microsoft knew that “unlike a lot of our competition, sending your most sensitive files down to a local machine into a VM was a complete nonstarter” — an apparent reference to Anthropic’s Claude Cowork, which runs in a virtual machine on the user’s computer.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella pitched Copilot as a hedge against relying on any one AI lab, saying companies should be able to test models against their own benchmarks and swap one out for another.

“My test of true independence going forward is for you to have a private eval that you can hill climb on and substitute a model,” he said. Translation: a “private eval” is a company’s own set of tests for AI models, and “hill climb” is a phrase in vogue in AI circles for steadily improving results against those tests.
A company that can’t do those things, he added, has effectively handed the knowledge it builds with AI “to somebody else.”

Model choice: Microsoft also emphasized the ability to switch between AI models from different companies. A menu shown during the presentation let users pick OpenAI’s GPT or Anthropic’s Opus, or an Auto mode that chooses a model for each request.
Microsoft also showed its own MAI models alongside OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI on one of Nadella’s slides, although they weren’t listed in the menu shown during the demo.

The rollout: Nadella first promised the super app at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in June, saying that “come summer” the company would bring “coding to all knowledge work within one Copilot super app.” On Microsoft’s July 29 earnings call , he told investors it would arrive “this quarter,” which ends Sept. 30.
Friday’s announcement meets that deadline with less than a week to spare, and most of the new features won’t be widely available until later.
Office inside Copilot: Copilot has long run inside Word, Excel and PowerPoint. Now the full apps also run inside Copilot. “This is not just some simplified viewer,” Andreou said.

In a demo, a Microsoft product manager had Copilot pull data into an Excel workbook, accepted her team’s tracked changes in a Word document, and then had Copilot turn both into a PowerPoint deck without leaving the app. Co-workers can edit the same files at the same time from the regular Office apps, according to Microsoft.

How it’s priced: Copilot now has two ways to pay. A per-user monthly license covers everyday uses such as chat and Copilot features in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams. More intensive agent work, including Cowork, Code and Autopilot, is billed based on usage, as are the newest frontier models, OpenAI’s Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Fable.

“Our view is that there are two kinds of AI at work,” said Jared Spataro, Microsoft’s chief marketing officer for AI at Work, in a recorded briefing for media. “They call for two very different ways of paying, and Copilot offers both.”
Consumer Microsoft 365 subscriptions will also add usage-based billing later this year for Cowork, Code and other new features, Spataro said.

Nadella told investors in July that Microsoft is evolving its business model “beyond per-seat to per-seat-plus-consumption.” Usage-based services are off by default, and administrators can set spending limits for an entire company, specific groups or individual users through Microsoft’s Agent 365 management tools.

From OpenClaw to Autopilot: Autopilot grew out of Microsoft’s experiments with OpenClaw, the open-source personal AI agent that went viral earlier this year. In March, Nadella described OpenClaw as a security risk akin to “a virus.”

By June, Microsoft had introduced Scout, an always-on personal agent for work that it called the first of its Autopilots. Nadella told investors in July that the agent was “powered by OpenClaw.” The new Copilot drops the Scout name, and people instead create and name their own Autopilots.
In his presentation this week, Andreou pitched Autopilot as the answer to the concerns that have kept agents like OpenClaw out of big companies.
“The hallmark of an amazing, long-running agent is autonomy and flexibility,” he said. “That is the same thing that makes them absolutely terrifying to an IT admin.”
Each Autopilot runs in the cloud inside a company’s Microsoft 365 environment, with its own identity, memory and email address, and people can tag it in Teams or Outlook like a co-worker.

In a demo, a Microsoft employee playing the role of a regional manager at a retail chain gave his Autopilot, named Dot, one goal: make sure stores had inventory in time for Black Friday. It chose which Teams channels, email threads and inventory data to monitor, sent him a daily summary, and flagged a shipment problem that could affect 18 stores.

The adoption question: Microsoft reported more than 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats in July, up from 20 million in April. That’s still only about 7% of the more than 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats the company reported in January.

The new Copilot comes three weeks after Microsoft reorganized its financial reporting around a similar idea, creating a segment called Agents and Infra and moving GitHub’s cloud revenue into its Microsoft 365 business.
“It’s no longer about building or selling one app or service, but about connecting the entire trajectory of a ‘job to be done,'” Nadella wrote in a note to investors about the change at the time.

Microsoft 365 cloud revenue, which covers business and consumer subscriptions including Copilot and now GitHub, reached $100.3 billion in fiscal 2026 under the new structure, up about 19%. Microsoft doesn’t disclose how much of that comes from Copilot.
“None of these things really matter unless they actually go to work inside of your companies and deliver real value,” Andreou said.
Microsoft plans to share more at its Ignite conference, Nov. 17-20 in San Francisco.

articles.title: Artists, game designers and producers hit hard as Microsoft cuts 277 jobs in Washington state
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft cut 277 jobs in the Seattle region as part of its latest round of layoffs, with artists, game designers and producers making up a large share of the affected roles, a new filing shows.

The filing was made public Thursday afternoon under the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act. Microsoft gave approximate numbers earlier this week when it announced the cuts , which included the latest stage in the company’s ongoing Xbox restructuring .
Art, game production, game design, technical art and audio design account for 77 of the 277 positions listed in the filing. Software engineering is the largest single category, totaling 60 roles.
Other positions are in functional areas including product marketing, technical writing, product management, data science, business management, finance and legal.

The filing says 252 of the positions impacted in the state are based at Microsoft’s Redmond campus, with 25 held by remote employees in the region, adding up to the 277 total. Microsoft had previously said about 300 of the cuts were in Washington state, out of fewer than 600 globally.

Out of that global total, 268 were in Xbox Game Studios, part of a restructuring designed to return the games division to growth and profitability. Halo Studios in Redmond faced a substantial reduction, and the company said work on the next Halo game is moving to its Activision subsidiary.
Microsoft cut 605 Washington jobs in July as part of 4,800 layoffs worldwide at the time. The company eliminated more than 15,000 positions globally across two rounds in 2025.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: New Train Day!
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: 2026 has been a big year for trains in Puget Sound. In January, the Federal Way Link Extension completed its first full month of operation. Simulated service on the 2 Line began in February , providing 4 minute frequencies for the first time between Seattle and Lynnwood. In March, the Crosslake Connection finally connected the 2 Line with Seattle. Link ridership jumped 46% in April thanks to the new service across Lake Washington. In May, the Sound Transit Board confirmed funding for several ST3 Link extensions (at the cost of other extensions). In June, Sound Transit welcomed passengers aboard new Sounder trains and set multiple Link ridership records . The USA vs Belgium World Cup match in early July helped Link surpass 300,000 passengers in one day for the first time ever. Last month, transit agencies in Snohomish, King, and Pierce counties restructured their bus networks to cement Link as the backbone for regional transportation in Puget Sound.
To add to the list, Sound Transit is opening a new Link station and Amtrak is rolling out next-generation trains in September.

On September 30, Amtrak Cascades will welcome the first passengers aboard new Amtrak Airo trainsets. Amtrak Airo are trains built by Siemens that will soon run on many short distance Amtrak routes across the country. The first three of eight trains for the Cascades route are in Seattle and will operate on two roundtrips daily. The remaining five trainsets will enter service as they complete testing. An additional 75 Amtrak Airo trainsets will begin serving other routes around the country next year.

While the new trains will not reduce travel times or offer more daily trips, these trains can carry more passengers (over 300 seats per train), will be more reliable, and are more comfortable than the aging rolling stock currently used on Amtrak Cascades. Passengers can expect adjustable headrests, panoramic windows, enhanced lighting, and modern interiors.
Beginning September 30, Amtrak Airo trains will be used on the following Amtrak Cascades trips.
Between Seattle and Eugene: Train 503: Seattle to Eugene at 7:10am – 1:48pm Train 508: Eugene to Seattle at 4:30pm – 10:50pm
Between Seattle and Vancouver: Train 516: Seattle to Vancouver, B.C. at 8:30am – 12:30pm Train 519: Vancouver, B.C. to Seattle at 4:45pm – 9:10pm

Seattle Transit Blog will share a first look at the Amtrak Airo trains next week, including pictures and videos from a trip on the train. Let us know in the comments if there are any specific features or amenities you would like to learn more about.

Also on September 30, Sound Transit will begin service at Pinehurst station. Pinehurst station is the agency’s first Link in-fill station and is located between Northgate and Shoreline South/148th stations. This the second piece of the ST3 measure to be completed (after Downtown Redmond Link) and will be the last Link station to open until Graham Street station in 2031. Pinehurst station is served by the new Metro Route 77 which connects the station with Bitter Lake and Lake City. 1 Line and 2 Line trains will begin stopping at Pinehurst station at 5am on September 30. The very first train to serve Pinehurst is a 2 Line train that departs Wilburton at 4:04am and arrives at Pinehurst at 5:05am.

To celebrate the new station, Sound Transit is hosting an event from 2pm-6pm on Wednesday. The event will include live music, local organizations, sponsors, food, an interactive activity with station artist Romson Bustillo, and the ST Shop merchandise booth.

articles.title: Dow Constantine Secures Three-Year Extension as Sound Transit CEO
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: The Sound Transit Board of Directors voted unanimously to grant agency CEO Dow Constantine a three-year extension on his contract on Thursday. Sound Transit Board Chair Dave Somers made the motion and spoke highly of Constantine's work.

"I've been around public service long enough to know strong, steady leadership matters, especially when the work is difficult and the stakes are high," Somers said. "And Dow has earned our confidence. Retaining him for the longer term is the right decision for this agency, our staff, and for this region."

In addition to extending Constantine's contract through the end of 2029, the motion also stipulates terms for two one-year extensions that could leave Constantine at the helm through 2031. If the agency does not exercise those extensions or fires him without cause, it will need to pay a severance package amounting to 18 months of pay.

As Snohomish County Executive, Somers noted the work to keep Everett Link on schedule – even as other light rail expansion projects rail face big delays after a budget reckoning vote in May – was high on list of Constantine's achievements in his first 18 months in office. Everett Link recently hit an important milestone , with the release of the Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS), which opened a public comment period and pushed the project a step closer to a final design.

"I want to take a moment to recognize some of what Sound Transit has accomplished under Dow's leadership," Somers said. "Opened the 2 Line crosslake connection. Provide highly reliable operations for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the largest operational test in the agency's history, successfully navigating the Enterprise Initiative and closing a $34 billion funding gap, and then immediately taking action on the steps outlined in the updated system plan. Opening Federal Way Link ahead of schedule, preparing to open the Pinehurst Station, our system's first infill station, which will be happening in just a very short time, advancing West Seattle and Everett Link through critical planning milestones, improved rider experience with increased ambassadors, wayfinding and security measures with fair gates coming soon as well, significantly reducing unplanned service disruptions through a new preventive maintenance program, all the while overseeing one of the most complicated and ambitious capital development programs in the entire country. Don't forget Everett Link DEIS [released] for public comment."

Sound Transit is still hoping to open the first segment of Everett Link (as far as Paine Field) by 2037, only one year later than promised in the Sound Transit 3 (ST3) ballot measure. The timelines for most other ST3 projects have fared much worse. For example, the northern half of Ballard Link (originally pledged to open in 2035) is at risk of a 25-year delay if the agency doesn't massively cut costs or find new revenue.
While delays have been most acute in the King County segment, King County Executive Girmay Zahilay echoed Somers' sentiment and gave Constantine high marks.

"Dow is doing an exceptional job, and so is his team," Zahilay said. "I'm very excited to be able to renew the contract and look forward to the continued leadership to deliver on behalf of the people of the Puget Sound region to build a regional transit system that we can all be proud of. And I think through all of the challenges that this agency has faced, both Dow and the chair have been doing a tremendous job, and I'm honored to be able to vote yes today."

After a long run with Peter Rogoff as CEO, Sound Transit had a bit of carousel in leadership. Julie Timm took over in 2022, coming over from Greater Richmond Transit Company in Virginia, but she lasted just 16 months before resigning , with some on the board growing dissatisfied with her leadership.

Former Seattle Department of Transportation head Goran Sparrman took the reins in an interim capacity in 2024, while the agency launched a national search. As that search dragged on, Sparrman informed the board he'd stay on no later than May 15, 2025. The board finally landed on their decision and found they did not need to look nationally, or even beyond their ranks for the leader they sought . Constantine took over on April 1, 2025.

The contract approved Thursday doubles down on Sound Transit's leader and the approach the agency has hewed to for the previous decade. Constantine was one of the chief architects of the ST3 package, which will push the agency to 116 miles of light rail when completed, and he'll continue to guide its buildout through a pivotal time.

During the public comment period of the meeting, a few transit advocates expressed frustration with the course Sound Transit is on and doubling down on that approach. Save Ballard Rail organizers like Carl Aslund expressed worries the project was getting left behind and buried.

"So how about that Ballard EIS? I believe that one was supposed to come out in October," Aslund said. "We'd love to get a date for when that's being released, and we'd also love to hear a date for a public forum in Ballard, so that the rest of our community who is unable to call in during work hours could all also learn more about what's going on."

In response to that call from advocates, Constantine did share that a Ballard public forum will occur on Monday, October 19, although the exact time and location are still to be determined. The project's long-delayed DEIS has been hung up in FTA review, with the Trump Administration appearing to give more scrutiny to an urban rail line compared to a suburban one.
In his brief remarks after securing the extension, Constantine underscored his passion for the work and set an ambitious goal of building the finest transit system in the United States.

"I can tell you now that you've completed the vote that I'm passionately dedicated to this work, and as I said a year or so ago, I will say again, I would do it for free," Constantine said. "So, but I'm glad you voted for the contract. So I look forward to continuing to build this organization, deliver the system that the voters approved, and really raise up the level of service, the quality of the service that the people are receiving, to make this the finest transit system in the country."

While Constantine joked he'd do the work for free, his compensation, by design, was in line with peers. Sound Transit staff did a market study that found that Constantine's half a million base salary is in line with comparable transit CEOs, the board motion notes.

In December, the board offered Constantine a merit-based raise, which he had deferred, though his contract does include cost-of-living adjustments throughout its term and further opportunities for merit pay. Additionally, the board awarded the CEO a $30,000 performance bonus, which he had previously deferred.

"On December 18, 2025, through Motion No. M2025-66, the Board gave Mr. Constantine a performance rating of outstanding based on his work in achieving his 2025 performance goals and objectives, however, a merit increase to his base salary and a discretionary annual contribution performance award were deferred at the CEO’s request," the board motion states.

Starting April 1, 2027, Constantine's annual base salary will grow to $490,086, with a 4% cost of living adjustments lined up annually, plus a business travel expense account and generous package of benefits, including nearly $100,000 in retirement benefit contributions annually, some of which is required by law.

One area where the board scaled back their initial proposed offer was on paid vacation time. The motion had initially offered 45 days of paid time off, but an amendment from Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello reduced annual paid time off to 35 days, the same as the current contract offers.

Contract settled, Constantine will now have three to five years to put his head down and try to whip a troubled ST3 package in shape, despite enormous near-term headwinds from a transit-averse Trump Administration and rising construction costs. With transit grants essentially impossible to come by under Trump 2.0, the agency will need to be ready to strike when new leadership takes over, theoretically, in 2029.

In the meantime, one thing the CEO will be doing less of is overseeing light rail openings, with no planned ribbon-cuttings after Pinehurst next week currently on the calendar until the Graham Street infill station in 2031.

The agency's delivery focus in the next three years will be the Stride bus rapid transit program, which the ST3 measure had promised in 2024, but the three lines have slipped four years behind schedule . Stride will stretch from Burien to Bellevue (S1 Line), from Bellevue to Lynnwood (S2 Line), and from Shoreline to Bothell (S3). The S2 is the most behind schedule and is slated to open in 2029 .

articles.title: Everett, Community Transit Lay Out Long-Awaited Transit Consolidation Plan
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Everett residents look to be on the cusp of a major expansion of local bus service, after the release of a proposed interlocal agreement that spells out a clear path for the city-run Everett Transit system to be annexed into Community Transit . On top of creating a more integrated transit network for riders, the move would provide the resources for a 50% increase in overall bus service in Everett, including more frequent routes and service extending much later into the evening.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Under the draft agreement released Wednesday, Everett Transit would be consolidated into the much larger Community Transit system next April, with an 18-month transition period to follow. The current 0.6% sales tax rate that funds Everett Transit would increase to 1.2%, bringing it in line with the rest of the county. The City of Everett would receive a one-time payment of $54.5 million for its transit assets, which include the Everett Station transit hub, and transfer $16 million in currently held reserves to fund future equipment and vehicle replacements.

"First and foremost, it's the only way to grow our transit system to meet the needs of our fast-growing communities," Everett Mayor Cassie Franklin said in announcing the agreement alongside Community Transit CEO Ric Ilgenfritz. "It's going to increase our transit capacity, and that keeps light rail on track, and that is a priority for all of us to get people off of I-5 and into public transportation that serves the region. And it's going to protect all of the transportation services within Everett that we have so many people relying on."

The annexation still needs to be approved by both the Everett City Council and the Community Transit Board of Directors, with potential votes set for early November following a pair of public hearings. But thanks to a 2025 change in state law, it would not need to be approved by voters, moving forward as soon as those two votes take place.

If given the green light, Community Transit would start work on an integrated network plan shortly after passage, with the existing Everett Transit network a baseline that the agency has to "maintain or exceed" service levels across. Starting in March of 2028, additional service would ramp up, with the full 50% increase in service levels required to be implemented by 2030.

"For Everett residents, this is going to be longer hours of operations. It's going to be more bus service hours, more busses operating within the city of Everett, shorter wait times, more direct routes, more connections – not just within Everett, but throughout the county," Franklin said.

Community Transit will commit to maintain the existing Swift Blue Line between Everett and Shoreline, and continue planning for its next bus rapid transit project, the Gold Line between Everett, Marysville, and Arlington that is on track to open in 2031. The agency also promises to add one on-demand microtransit service area in Everett, adding to existing Zip Shuttle zones that are already in place in Darrington, Lake Stevens, Arlington, and Lynnwood's Alderwood neighborhood.

Everett Transit's $2 adult fare and $0.50 fare for seniors and people with disabilities – slightly lower than Community Transit's respective $2.50 and $1 fares – will be required to be maintained for a period of at least one year.

One point of contention around this potential merger has been paratransit service, the on-demand shuttle service for people with disabilities that transit agencies are required to provide under federal law. Everett Transit provides its paratransit services in-house, with Community Transit instead utilizing contractors through bus operator TransDev. In addition, Everett Transit has long gone beyond its basic requirements around who receives paratransit service, including the entire city within the service area rather than limiting it to a specific distance from fixed-route transit, and including all Everett residents over 65 years old.

Under the agreement, Community Transit agrees to maintain service for all existing Everett Transit paratransit customers, using existing Everett Transit vehicles "for as long as practical." New customers who previously would have qualified for paratransit service in Everett based on age would not be able to enroll in the program.

In spite of the clear benefits that could come from service expansion, the idea of a merger has vocal critics within Everett, including from a contingent of Everett Transit employees. Wrapped up in concerns over job security – and opposition to a sales tax increase – is the idea that Everett would lose direct control over how service in the city operates.

"Things will fall through the cracks with Community Transit that don't with Everett," Everett Transit operator Daryle Sullivan told the Everett Council in August. "Right now you can walk out of your door and walk two blocks and get to a bus stop, and that'll get you eventually to Everett Station where you're set. Community Transit – that's not what they specialize in. We do. We can't do what Community Transit does. They can't do what we do. Keep everyone in their lane, doing what they do best and specialize in."

In contrast, Ilgenfritz framed the benefits of an integrated network as a major upgrade for Everett residents. In his six-year run as Community Transit CEO , he has overseen a transit agency that has been able to eclipse 2019 ridership levels by increasing service and capitalizing on the expansion of light rail into Snohomish County.

"The things that excite me about this are the trips that can't be taken today, or are very difficult for any regular person to use today," Ilgenfritz said, noting that it's nearly impossible for an employee at Everett's major employment centers of Providence Hospital, the Navy Yard, or the Port of Everett to get to their job if they live elsewhere in the county. "We have an opportunity to break down those inefficiencies in the network and create direct connections between all of the other cities in this county and those employment centers, and that's what's going to be so essential for this city and this county to compete in the global economy in the years ahead."

Ultimately, the shift from Everett Transit to Community Transit would represent a major change, with one of the state's last city-run transit agencies disappearing. But from a rider perspective, the transition plan unveiled this week provides a path to making that change as painless as possible for riders.

"If we do our jobs right, the employees of Everett Transit, customers of Everett Transit, won't see any changes in their service as the ownership of that responsibility for providing public transit in Everett shifts from the city to us," Ilgenfritz said. "If you are an Everett Transit user today, the service you see out there on the road today will be there after this takes effect. And once we get through that planning process we talked about, it will start to get better."

Transit riders and residents will be able to weigh in on the proposed merger at a public hearing at the Everett City Council on October 28, and at the Community Transit board on October 29. Votes would come one week later.

articles.title: The flock thickens: Starbird Chicken is coming to Capitol Hill
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: $5 A MONTH TO HELP KEEP CHS PAYWALL-FREE Subscribe to CHS to help hire writers and photographers to cover the neighborhood. CHS is a pay what you can community news site with no required sign-in or paywall. To stay that way, we need you. Become a subscriber to help us cover the neighborhood for $5 a month -- or choose your level of support (Image: Starbird Chicken)

The mystery of new commercial life hatching in the failed 10,000-square-foot Amazon grocery on E Pike has been revealed. The arrival of Starbird Chicken on Capitol Hill will mark new energy for a block that has been darkened for two and a half years.

It will also be an example of what happens when highly optimized, fully leveraged, and fluidly designed corporate strategies cross lines, overlap, and push all their eggs into the same basket in a neighborhood with finger lickin good demographics and spending habits.

“Starbird has built something truly special by reimagining what a chicken restaurant can be, from the bold flavors and hospitable, modern restaurant design to the overall guest experience,” Vin Mehta , the Portland-based entrepreneur and franchisee leading a 17 location expansion of the chicken chain into the Pacific Northwest, said in a company press release quoted by industry tracker FastCasual.com . “Together, we’ll combine Starbird’s innovative approach with our team’s operational experience and passion for building lasting connections.”

CHS reported this summer on signs of new life in the Pike at Belmont space in the AVA Capitol Hill mixed-use redevelopment of the neighborhood’s old Mercedes-Benz dealership where the massive Amazon Go was abruptly shuttered in 2024 as part of what would become a nationwide retreat for the global giant.

This week, Starbird’s construction team filed new paperwork with details of their plans for a new 3,000-square-foot restaurant to serve the company’s tenders, wings, and sandwiches in a major chunk of the former cashier-less, tech-powered grocery space. An ambitious $620,000 base construction budget is attached.
The expansion has already been on the burner. A West Seattle Starbird is scheduled for its ribbon cutting on Fauntleroy Way SW on Monday .

Starbird is a Northern California-born, premium fast-casual restaurant chain founded in 2016 by culinary incubator The Culinary Edge , a company that operates as a gun for hire in revamping menus and operations for large national chains while also establishing its own brands.

Starbird specializes in “fresh, scratch-made food” and “always antibiotic-free, never frozen” fried chicken including tenders, sandwiches, wings, and “house-made sauces,” positioning itself around “reinventing the fast-food experience” with “feel good crispy chicken.” With an emphasis on “tech-enabled, omnichannel dining” and virtual kitchens alongside brick-and-mortar restaurants, the brand has expanded beyond California through multi-unit franchise partnerships.
The name also has a familiar ring. Yes, it sounds like Starbucks . And, hey, we’re not sure what the folks at the 1910-era Starbird Apartments around the block on Boylston will think.
One of the most recent Starbird openings was in Colorado (Image: Starbird Chicken)

The first Starbird opened in 2016 in Sunnyvale, California, on W El Camino Real a few miles from Apple Park and a shorter drive from the LinkedIn headquarters. The Silicon Valley debut served as the pilot location for the concept, testing their app-based curbside pickup model alongside standard dine-in service. Like most big chains, in-store ordering is heavily automated via digital kiosks and integrated mobile app check-ins.

Starbird’s traditional real estate footprint favors car-oriented, suburban-style corridors over dense, pedestrian neighborhoods but there a few different formats of stores. In San Francisco, Starbird developed a commercial ghost kitchen hub in SoMa, serving the area through bike and scooter couriers and delivery apps.
Capitol Hill, circa 2026 and 2027, is up to its ears in chicken joints. And the flock is growing even with the now permanent loss of neighborhood favorite Bok a Bok .

This month, CHS reported plans from Puget Sound-based Conscious Hospitality Group for a re-start of its 11th Ave restaurant space with a new roasted chicken venture fronted by celebrity influencer chef Matt Broussard . The Seattle Times gushed over the prospects but didn’t report that the plan is a re-heat. The 11th Ave space was originally the flagship location of the company’s scuttled “1,000 location,” sustainable, and tech-optimized chicken sandwich chain concept Mt. Joy.
Starbird, meanwhile, has pushed past the 20 location mark and is on a skyward trajectory.

“From day one, we saw something special in Starbird. This innovative concept is in a league all its own,” investor Greg Dollarhyde said in an announcement five years ago as the company raised $12 million in funding. “Starbird continues to beat every expectation.”
Starbird Capitol Hill is under construction at 600 E Pike. Learn more at starbirdchicken.com .

articles.title: Here are your chances to speak up on the mayor’s proposal to overcome Seattle’s $175M deficit
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The Seattle City Council has launched its review of Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed $9.1 billion 2027–2028 budget, scheduling multiple hearings and public comment opportunities over the next two months before adopting a final plan.

Councilmember Dan Strauss , chair of the Select Budget Committee, emphasized community participation as the council evaluates funding priorities. Residents can weigh in during six regular comment sessions and two dedicated public hearings featuring both remote and in-person testimony.

CHS reported here on the Wilson proposal which would wipe out an inherited $175 million deficit without tax increases or withdrawals from city reserves. The proposal would cut roughly $50 million annually in General Fund spending by eliminating 128 positions and aligning departmental budgets with historical costs, pairing these cuts with $50 million in shuffled funding — primarily leveraging JumpStart payroll tax revenues to cover core services and homelessness programs — and enabling the city, Wilson says, to project balanced budgets through 2030 without drawing on reserves.
The council’s announcement invites the public to review the council’s Budget Basic webpage to “learn more about how they can make their voice heard.”

articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The city officially proclaimed September 25th as “Dolly Parton Day” to celebrate the legendary artist and philanthropist’s contributions to music, culture, and childhood literacy following her passing in August.
City Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck presented the proclamation during a tribute story hour at the Queen Anne Library branch.
In August , the AIDS Memorial Pathway Plaza above Capitol Hill Station was the gathering place for a vigil following Parton’s death at age 80.

The September 25th date serves as a nod to Parton’s iconic hit “9 to 5.” Citywide celebrations also feature a silent disco and a screening of 9 to 5 at Denny Park, honoring Parton’s program that has provided nearly 4.5 million free books to Washington children.

articles.title: Slog AM: Money for Dow Constantine, Trump and Xi Do Nothing, and Vivian Says Goodbye to Seattle
articles.author: Vivian McCall
paras: I am leaving The Stranger . Before the keyboard warriors get too excited, there’s no palace intrigue here. I’m not ragequitting, fleeing, or resigning in protest. I even sat on the hiring committee for a new Editor in Chief, who I expect to be announced soon. I’m not even leaving the company. I’m transferring to The Chicago Reader , and moving back to the city I love the most, where my entire family lives, where I spent a large portion of every childhood summer, where I attended college, and where I started my career. And if I can be honest, I missed the mild winters. I’ll save my sappy thoughts for the end.

[Editor’s Note: IS VIVIAN MAKING A MISTAKE?? The Oxford Economics’ 2026 Global Cities Index ranked Seattle the fourth best city to live and visit. The cities were ranked on “governance, economics, human capital, environment, and quality of life.” Hm. Chicago isn’t even in the top 10. It’s 47th on the list.]
Editor, you fail to consider the dying planet. Chicago is ranked the best city in the world for climate preparedness .

What the fuck is happening to 15th Avenue? We lost Ada’s Cafe, Michelangelo could’ve painted half a Sistine Chapel in the time Coastal Kitchen’s replacement, Fire Tacos and Cantina, has been in the works, the best part of the street, the Punk Rock Flea Market, has limited time on this earth, and now three restaurants have gone dark at once. Cedar mentioned this yesterday, but it bears repeating because, well, this is my street, it’s personal to me, and there’s a tad more information.

First reported by Capitol Hill Seattle Blog , Rione XIII, Rubinstein Bagels are permanently closed, and Bar Vacilando is closing up shop on Saturday. After years of leaks, unstable brickwork, “and trouble reliably controlling the temperature in the spaces,” the restaurant group that owns Rubinstein Bagels and Rione XIII, One House Hospitality, told The Seattle Times it wasn’t “comfortable” continuing to operate with the rainy season ahead.

On Monday, a judge will reexamine whether Christopher Leahy, charged with murder for allegedly stabbing 19-year-old University of Washington student Juniper Blessing more than 40 times this May, is competent to stand trial. According to a June psychological evaluation, Leahy had a well-documented history of psychosis and schizophrenia, and determined he was not competent to stand trial at that time.

Blessing was transgender, but the King County Prosecutor’s office said there was no evidence her murder was motivated by hate. If such evidence is found, prosecutors can consider additional charges, KUOW reports.

Two kids from Redmond who went missing in December 2023 were found in Washington DC last week. As is usually the case, the kidnapper was a parent . The children’s father reported them missing in May 2024, months after he’d last seen them. A temporary parenting plan had expired and the children’s mother had not returned the children after losing custody. The mother fled with her kids and concealed their names to avoid the cops and the feds.
ICYMI: The wickedly talented Adele Dazeem Amanda Manitach interviewed painter Kelly Bjork, whose show, Lunacy , will be at the J. Rinehart Gallery tomorrow through October 28. Check it out .

Christmas came early for Sound Transit CEO and former County Executive Dow Constantine, who was awarded a $30,000 bonus, a near $16,000 salary bump, and a new three-year contract (he’ll also get a 4 percent inflation boost in April). It’s been a big time for the transit agency. During the World Cup, the light rail saw its highest-ever ridership numbers, and Sound Transit just opened up the cross-lake connection, which, dead fish aside, has been a success. Constantine’s salary starting January 1 will be $490,086. Happy New Year to you, Dow, hope that’s enough.

What the hell? A 700-pound sea lion was found dead near the mouth of the Duwamish River in West Seattle. X-rays revealed numerous “projectiles” in its body. “What made this case particularly unusual was the number of projectiles found in the animal,” writes KING 5. “This is the most projectiles I have seen in one body. Probably in my entire career of doing this,” said a representative of the marine mammal response and rehabilitation organization. The “projectiles” were bullets, and this was not a legal hunting situation. I know just the detective for the case. Fuck with animals in this town, and you release the wolf.

Two authoritarians wrapped up their state visit with a peek at the Constitution and the Bill of Rights, the Associated Press reports. Chinese President Xi Jinping heads home after his three-day trip to hang with US President Donald Trump, his first visit to DC in a decade. They made no breakthroughs on trade or the safety of artificial intelligence.

A third global asshole, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was in New York to “rage against” his critics , including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, at the UN General Assembly. More than 100 people, including actors Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder, were detained for protesting outside. He said that allegations of genocide in Gaza were the “biggest lie of the century” and defending attacking Iran with the US as one of the “easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make.”

The Government Accountability Office said the Trump administration wasted millions of dollars on his evil immigration detention crusade. One could argue the whole thing was a waste of money, but the Office found $3 million dollars spent on unused tents to house migrants at Guantanamo Bay, $20.5 million on administrative costs and utilities in seven warehouses the government bought and sold, and $7.1 million in food “it did not need” for detention camps in Texas. The New York Times has more .
Nathalie here cutting in with some quick breaking news.

The Supreme Court will let Trump use federal data system for citizenship checks : The Trump administration can now use its expanded federal data system to check the citizenship of voter rolls, ruled the Supreme Court . The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements data system, SAVE, will allow the administration to continue its search for noncitizens and its quest for compiling a master database of US adult citizens in each state. Critics worry that SAVE violates privacy rights and that it is inaccurate and has flagged citizens as noncitizens.

Back to me, with news that a vicious nor’easter will pound the northeast coast with rain, wind, and waves through the weekend. “Waves up to 19 feet have been recorded already along North Carolina’s Outer Banks. Waves up to 12 feet are possible from the Outer Banks to the New Jersey shore through Saturday, and along the New England coast through Sunday,” reports ABC News .

Iran suggested a deal to resume nuclear talks and reopen the Strait of Hormuz in seven days if, and only if, the US lifts its naval blockade, waives sanctions on Iranian oil, and agrees to a ceasefire in Iran and Lebanon. With the midterms approaching, they see an opportunity, though Trump says he is in no rush to make a deal.

So, this is it, huh? Seattle has been good to me, and so has The Stranger . I’m proud of the work I’ve done here, particularly of my beat coverage on trans people. I came to The Stranger because I saw an opportunity to report accurately on one of the minority groups that has become a target of fascist violence and propaganda. My background was not in LGBTQ journalism—I entered the field reporting on science and medicine —but I had a hard time watching the mainstream media screw up trans stories on the regular. I’ve seen bungled science, omitted context around extremist politics and policy, and a basic failure to grasp the trans struggle in America. Our primary concerns are not misgendering and a lack of validation. Most of us are poor, we want healthcare just like everybody else, and some people—the real freaks—want to hurt us.

We’re not the overly sensitive bunch that assholes say we are. We’re tough and a lot of us are funny as fuck. Shameless plug: This zine I worked on with my hilarious friends, Cosmo t-girl . Issue 2 is on the way and I am way behind on my obligations to you all, sorry. (Another shameless plug: I make music as Pansy. Our Instagram handle is @pansysucks but I do not think we suck .)

I don’t put much stock in awards when it comes to my own work— they are not in the top 20 reasons I am in this profession—but the judge’s comments on my first-place Association of Alternative Newsweeklies (AAN) award for beat reporting perfectly summed up what I’d been trying to do for years: “Though the topic is often grim, the writer doesn’t shy away from being irreverent, or even funny, where appropriate. Any alt weekly that wants to start a trans beat (which I would argue is vital today) should use these stories to show the way forward.” Damn, thanks, whoever that was.
To my coworkers, I really will miss you. You’re all very funny, smart, and you give a shit. I could hardly ask for more. Oh, and Shon Barnes? I can’t wait to go to the Bean with you in Chicago.

articles.title: The Newsfeed's "Follow-up Week"
articles.author: Jaelynn Grisso
paras: The longest-running hotel workers’ strike in Washington’s history came to a close when Hilton and its workers agreed to a contract earlier this month. We previously reported on the workers’ efforts and concerns ahead of the World Cup. Now, we’re bringing you an update with what’s in the workers’ new contract.
The first strike Aspen Desmarais joined turned out to be historic.

“85 days was a lot. It was in the first couple of weeks. It was really fun. And then for a second there, it felt really hard fought and like what we were doing wasn't getting any impact. But I will not be out stubborn by anyone until I get the things that we need to protect people,” said Desmarais, a bartender at Embassy Suites by Hilton.

Desmarais and other workers went on strike on June 18th during the FIFA Men’s World Cup. The strike lasted a total of 85 days. The union hopes the contract agreement will pave the way for other hotel workers in the state.
Some of the changes in the new agreement include:

Hilton responded to a request for comment, saying: “This agreement reflects a collaborative outcome and our commitment to our valued Team Members. We look forward to welcoming our Team Members back to work and continuing to deliver exceptional hospitality to our guests.”
But for Desmarais, perhaps the biggest win was laying the groundwork to help protect immigrant workers.

“When people come to online commenting about our immigrant workers and being saying that they shouldn't be afraid if they're legal, they are all legal. It's just a scary world and Ice does not care if you're legal or not... In an extremely oppressive system right now towards immigrants. I think any win is a win,” Desmarais said.

During our week of coverage on wage theft , we told you about t wo groups of bikini baristas suing their bosses . Now, a King County judge awarded one of the groups more than $1.85 million in back pay after finding the owner violated state labor law.
Mykie, who worked for Tagle for about a year, estimates she is owed between $10,000 and $15,000 in unpaid wages.

“It's a huge win, not only just for us in our class action lawsuit, but for workers everywhere. It doesn't matter what you wear as a work uniform. It doesn't matter what people's opinions are of the work that me and other women do. It’s still work at the end of the day, and we still deserve to be paid correctly for the work that we do,” said Mykie, who asked to only be identified by her first name.
The class action lawsuit involved 70 baristas who worked at 5 bikini coffee huts across King and Snohomish Counties owned by Alan Tagle between 2021 and 2024.

The Judge determined that Tagle did not issue paychecks to the baristas, nor regularly track their hours worked. And that Tagle implemented strict sales goals, and baristas said they were threatened with being scheduled for less desirable shifts or losing their jobs if they didn’t meet those goals.

“There were days where I went home with nothing. There were days where I put my own money from my purse that I brought. It was really standard practice to at least for me and some of the other women that I had worked with to bring our own cash, just in case we needed to put some money into the till. So, there were days where I actively lost money for working,” Mykie said.
Tagle’s lawyers didn’t respond to a request for comment.

His brother Johnathan Tagle, who also owns a string of bikini coffee huts, is facing a similar lawsuit. He is accused of not paying his workers in accordance with state law, and of sexually harassing them.
By a lot of measures, Seattle won the FIFA Men’s World Cup.

“I think the gross numbers were pleasingly surprising to us. I mean, when we see 548,000 people descend upon our downtown on any given day, that's pretty exciting,” said Chris Copacino, Vice President of Communications for the Downtown Seattle Association.

Local public radio station KUOW estimated that state and local entities spent $120 million to host six matches of the FIFA Men’s World Cup. From June 15 to July 6, Seattle’s downtown saw about 3 million domestic visitors over the three weeks, according to the Downtown Seattle Association. Match days saw about a 17% increase in foot traffic over those same days in 2025.
The numbers – based on cell phone data – didn’t include international visitors.
Copacino called it a success, with lessons to be learned for future big events.

“People, especially our members and and people in the community see what can happen when we activate public spaces, when we create great pedestrian walking experiences, when public and private partnerships come together just to make sure that our city shines and is ready to receive people,” Copacino said.

He said that another big takeaway is to ensure that other neighborhoods – such as the Chinatown-International District, or CID -- also see the benefits. Neighborhood activists in the CID had been concerned about how the FIFA World Cup games would affect the neighborhood – which often sees negative impacts such as traffic and congestion from stadium events without seeing much benefit. After the games began, the Chinatown-International District Business Improvement Area and others organized an official watch party in Hing Hay Park for the last game in Seattle, and held additional watch parties for later matches held in other cities.
“I think that making sure that all of our communities are in and around the stadium feel the excitement,” Copacino said. “We need to make sure that all of the neighborhoods are feeling this.”

Some local boosters hope the city can get a chance to apply these lessons if Seattle is one of the cities picked to host when 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup comes to the U.S., Mexico, Jamaica and Costa Rica.

With an increasing amount of anti-trans bills proposed nationwide – including two here in Washington – more trans people are relocating to Seattle. , As we reported in June, this prompted local advocates to raise the alarm that the influx is creating a crisis in available resources.

TRACTION, a nonprofit focused on trans and gender-queer individuals, began a program in 2023 called project Open Arms. It helps trans folks in so-called hostile states relocate to a safer place. So far, they’ve been able to help more than 100 people relocate and hundreds more with smaller requests, but TRACTION Executive Director C. Michael Woodward says the demand is much higher.

“There's been periods when we've been getting requests like ten or more a day. I think the last time I counted the total number of applications we've had is nearing 1,800. We haven't been able to help nearly that many people because we just have the capacity,” Woodward said.
Seattle’s LGBTQ Commission heard from community organizations about the crisis and brought concerns to the city in May.

Three months later, both the mayor’s office and city council dedicated funding to address the crisis. City Council passed a one-time funding measure to provide $300,000 to community organizations. The mayor’s office also approved an additional $450,000.
Woodward said the city hasn’t announced an application process for the funds yet, but if TRACTION receives part of that money, it will be going directly into trans folks hands.
TRACTION and a coalition of other queer and trans organizations also created a public survey to gather more information on the crisis.

“We want to help the city know, like what's going on here so that they really have data to be able to justify," Woodward said. “Because I know people [who say], ‘Oh, it's not a crisis.’ I'm like, well, it is a crisis. You know, a lot of people are really being threatened. And there's been death. You know, people have been killed. This is a crisis.”
Beyond the downtown hustle of Seattle’s Pioneer Square, inside the historic Metropole Building, lives a different kind of historical significance.
A new immersive and living archival space - the Seattle Black Panther Party Interpretive Center .
During our interview with Seattle Black Panther Party co-founder Elmer Dixon in February , he recounted his work to keep the chapter’s legacy alive.
Then, he also shared details about the center that was in the works to memorialize the group’s legacy.
This summer, the center opened to the public. Program manager Naudia Miller says it’s drawn a crowd from across the country.

“We opened up in June, but we've already had over 1,300 people join us this far in Pioneer Square,” Miller said. When guests walk into the modern and industrial space, on one wall, they're greeted by a chronological history of the Seattle Panthers: before its founding, after it, and up to the present day.

The gallery includes mixed mediums from paintings by local artists, to a documentary teaser about the Seattle comrades, to a sitting area near front entrance filled with shelves of Black non-fiction literature that Miller says was part of the Panthers’ reading list.

articles.title: It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already here | Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein
articles.author: Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein
paras: Israel and the US have used AI to kill in Gaza and Iran, while law enforcement uses it in surveillance and arrests. The future is here

In recent weeks, concerns about AI have forged unlikely alliances in the tech and policy worlds. Tech moguls such as Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis joined Dario Amodei, Satya Nadella and Bill Gates in sounding the alarm about the dangers of AI and called for a slowdown of the technology’s development despite years of racing for dominance. The senator Bernie Sanders teamed up with Steve Bannon to urge Congress to regulate AI, which has become one of the very few issues to unite Americans across the political spectrum.

The latest moves were sparked in part by the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’s warnings on Twitter/X that AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and believe that the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

articles.author: David Smith in Washington
paras: Experts and insiders explain how To Catch A Predator became the most controversial show on 2000s TV

A man from Long Beach, California, is here to have sex with someone he believes is a 13-year-old girl. When the journalist Chris Hansen walks in, the man’s stomach drops. He is caught, and it is the end of his life as he knew it. Hansen asks what his fate should be. “The electric chair?” he asks. No, replies Hansen. “Dateline NBC.”

This is the opening scene of Primetime , a film directed by Lance Oppenheim, released in the US this week (a UK release follows on 30 October). It explores how a network news show turned sting operations into must-see television, raising a host of ethical questions about justice, voyeurism and society’s willingness to dehumanise certain offenders for profit and entertainment.

articles.title: Taylor Swift: The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore review – flashes of humanity and bafflingly vindictive love songs
articles.author: Laura Snapes
paras: (Republic) This four-track addition to a critically maligned album works hard to remind fans what they love about Swift, with some sweet highs and galling lows

One downside of turning your release strategies into scavenger hunts and layering clues within your work is that it invites enormous amounts of scrutiny about your potential motive. When Taylor Swift announced an expanded edition of last year’s critically maligned The Life of a Showgirl this week, subtitled The Encore, many fans instantly suspected one of two things: that it was designed to remind Grammy members of Showgirl’s existence during their voting period to determine next year’s nominees, or to oust country ingenue Ella Langley from her record-breaking US No 1 run .

If that sounds cynical, it’s also worth remembering that when Swift announced Showgirl last year, she said that unlike her previous album, The Tortured Poets Department – a 16-track record immediately inflated to 31 songs on release day – the purposefully concise, 12-track Showgirl would not be expanded. (This didn’t stop her releasing 34 variants of the record, with various acoustic demos and so on, to juice sales.)

articles.title: Trump has gotten rid of many of the checks and balances that could stop him from demolishing the Kennedy Center
articles.author:
<name>E. Andrew Taylor, Associate Professor and Director of Arts Management, American University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/e-andrew-taylor-1252707"/>
paras: Who gets to decide the future of the living memorial to former President John F. Kennedy , and who holds those decision-makers to account?

This debate is becoming ever more fraught. A photo taken on Sept. 16, 2026 , showed President Donald J. Trump in Air Force One reviewing a poster with the words “Kennedy Center DEMOLISH …” that many interpreted to mean “demolished.”

The image spread quickly. Like the protests that brought throngs of arts lovers to the center a few days later , it amplified the drama around the fate of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C. For more than a half-century, the multivenue complex has featured world-class symphonies, operas, dance and theater performances, along with education programs.

Whether it would be open or closed to the public, active or dormant, repaired or dismantled, solvent or bankrupt and if it can include Trump’s name in its branding have been the subjects of widespread dispute and speculation since Trump returned to office.
As a professor and scholar of arts management , I can explain why the official answers to who gets to decide and who is supposed to hold those deciders accountable are reasonably clear.

Congress created the Kennedy Center and determines its governance . It’s up to lawmakers, through their power of the purse, to decide on funding for construction, repairs and a portion of its operational budget.

The oversight of facilities and programs falls to a board of trustees that’s authorized by Congress to advance the mission and secure the majority of the center’s earned and contributed revenue. And those operations are, in turn, subject to review by the Internal Revenue Service, which determines the center’s nonprofit status, and federal courts, which determine its compliance with the law.
So how did that hierarchy of oversight essentially collapse into a shouting match between Trump and Rep. Joyce Beatty , an Ohio Democrat, and result in two ongoing lawsuits in U.S. District Court?
Beatty filed one of the suits and a consortium of architects and preservationists filed the other. The same judge , Christopher R. Cooper, is presiding over both cases.
The main cause of what I would call a governance failure is that most of those official oversight authorities now serve at the pleasure of the president.

In 2025, the Republican-controlled Congress approved US$257 million for “necessary expenses for capital repair, restoration, maintenance backlog, and security structures” at the Kennedy Center. But most GOP legislators have remained silent about its oversight, including multiple attempts to affix Trump’s name to the building – which Judge Cooper keeps insisting is something only Congress can allow.
Trump has chaired its board of trustees and appointed the vast majority of its members since an unprecedented restructuring to the previously bipartisan board in February 2025.

In his May 2026 ruling , Judge Cooper found the board of trustees to be “derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center.” More recently, the DC Preservation League has suggested removal of the trustees and appointment of a receiver if current leadership “is unwilling or unable to exercise its fiduciary duty.”

With both Congress and the trustees aligned with Trump, there are several federal agencies that could be stepping in to critique the board or its decisions: the Internal Revenue Service, the Justice Department, the Office of Management and Budget and others.
But they are all cooperating with the White House in a dramatic consolidation of power by the executive branch that now reaches into traditionally independent federal agencies .

That leaves the federal courts, where Beatty is among the few with standing to sue. She is an ex officio member of the board , meaning that she serves by virtue of her role in Congress. She also is willing to stand up and challenge the Trump administration’s attempt to direct – and perhaps even demolish – the Kennedy Center.

Even as these and other construction-related lawsuits are pending, the Trump administration has proven its willingness and ability to build, renovate or destroy federal landmarks without clear authority to do so.

Trump had the White House East Wing demolished in October 2025 without getting Congress to sign off or sharing those plans in advance. And he has built a new helipad on White House grounds, to name two examples.

Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts has called Trump’s attempt to build a ballroom where the East Wing used to stand without congressional authorization “ likely unlawful .” And yet, construction continues.
The buildings on the Kennedy Center campus are only part of what’s at stake.

The Kennedy Center was established as a “living memorial” to former President John F. Kennedy. The “memorial” part is largely associated with the physical campus and its many engravings and artworks honoring Kennedy.

But the “living” component manifests in its live performances, original productions, educational programming, artistic leadership and what audiences, educators and students experience both within and beyond the campus walls.

There were early indicators that both programs and public engagement were faltering under the board’s new leadership. Revenue from performances began a steep decline after Trump’s takeover in February 2025, well before he announced his intention to close the center for major repairs . It wasn’t just audiences turning away – many artists also canceled their engagements or stopped making customary bookings.

Prior to that takeover, The Washington Post has reported, the center’s finances had become increasingly strong as it recovered from the disruptions that all arts venues suffered during the COVID-19 pandemic.

So, who gets to decide the future of this living memorial to a revered slain president ? In the short term, it’s the center’s board, chaired by Trump. And who holds those decision-makers to account? Ongoing federal court cases have constrained or delayed some of those choices. But most other official checks and balances are currently neutral or skewed in the president’s favor.

Public attention through independent journalism and citizen activism can increase friction and shape the political calculus surrounding the Kennedy Center. But any long-term solution will depend on the physical condition of its campus, its adherence to its original mission as a living memorial and the reliable, responsible and accountable governance of its leaders.
