articles.title: The Devil You Know
articles.author: Amanda Manitach
paras: Kelly Bjork’s imagery has always centered around scenes of domesticity and intimacy. Their paintings feel familiar because they document the often-overlooked details of everyday life: the pleasing pattern of repeating tile, the warm grain of wood floorboards, the cozy, curated clutter of a living room shelf. These scenes are familiar because we have lived there.

But beyond the narrative of tenderness and brick-and-mortar interiors, a larger picture emerges, traced in the titles of Bjork’s exhibitions spanning the past 15 years. In Blankets (2012–2015), a story of intimacy is told through the utilitarian household object folded, draped, and crumpled like a kind of semiotic origami. Just one image in the series reveals what’s implied: a person hidden within the folds. In Living Together (2017), the realm of objects is expanded, the solo towel-as-signifier giving way to rooms filled with things. Still, these are highly curated vignettes playing games of hide-and-seek. Each offers only a partial view of a living space, often containing a doorway or window into another secondary space where, again, we’re only allowed a smattering of information placed like clues: a desk where art is presumably made, a bed where sex is presumably had. In Almost Home (2015–2017), figures finally come into view: a meeting of unclothed women in a steamy sauna, a partner waiting alongside a grandmother’s deathbed, and self-portraits, often mirrored or bifurcated, as though teasing at developments to come. Gentle Cravings (2018) expands the imagery to scenes further afield from home: a therapist’s waiting room, a woman waiting on an apartment stoop, and other people’s couches, rugs, and rituals. In Anima Rising (2019), we are introduced to new beds with new and old lovers—with a candor that would make the Blankets blush. The show’s namesake piece is a self-portrait of Bjork on their knees, hair chopped, pendulous breasts hanging, with a second self rising up between the legs of another person. It’s feral and carnal. And they like it.

Bjork’s first solo exhibition with J. Rinehart Gallery in 2022, Swimming Naked , offers imagery at its most explicit, fleshy, and decidedly queer. It depicts scenes of lovers under the covers, gay friends and queens (there’s a cameo of Betty Wetter), and even an ass getting eaten out. Of course, the ass is eaten tenderly, as only Bjork can paint it. “Jump in, swim naked, the water is fine,” the statement beckons.

For their second show with J. Rinehart, titled Lunacy , Bjork has exited the temperature-controlled wading pools of queer joy to plunge into the deep end of some danker waters, as they reckon with disorientation, dissociation, and new connections forming in a new chapter of their life, on the cusp of perimenopause. Just when you think you’ve gotten to know your truest self, another side emerges.

Your work has charted personal transformations over the past 15 years. How do you describe your gender and sexuality now? (Or is that important?) BJORK: I do claim being queer, nonbinary, and trans. It does feel important to establish representation.

Do you think of your practice as more exhibitionist or diaristic? BJORK: I would say diaristic since it really is me documenting my life. Some of that may feel exhibitionistic at times, but that has felt necessary to paint the full picture (pun intended lol).

What does painting the full picture accomplish? BJORK: I feel that it allows my audience to fully connect with me. They may not have the same experiences and the work may not have the same meaning to them as it does to me, but I am so often told that it makes them feel something, and that is a very special way I can connect with people.
How do you choose what to depict in your images, and what remains private? BJORK: You know, I really don’t choose for anything to be private.
You don’t have images tucked away that will never see the light of day? BJORK: I don’t! I put it all out there!

What does “lunacy” mean to you? BJORK: The definition: “intermittent periods of insanity, such as were believed to be triggered by the moon’s cycle” was what really struck me in relating to this work. Experiencing perimenopause and the mental and physical struggles that come along with that truly do feel like pure insanity at times. And having a cycle that so often is tied to the moon just resonated. Lunacy also means foolishness to me, in relation to art making—I can feel in a state of madness when creating, and I have to be in it to fully feel myself, and I think that is an insanity in itself.

Has your definition of intimacy—or the way you think of it in your imagery—shifted over the years? BJORK: Yes, I think intimacy started out in my work meaning relationships with my loved ones, and that continued but changed focus on more of my relations to the queer community. In Lunacy, I feel like intimacy is shown by allowing the viewer to see me fumble through experiencing my body changing, my struggles with mental health, my coping mechanisms, and also through what I grasp and seek to find hope and keep going.

Who is this work for? Previously, the work has been focused on making that tender, safe moment for viewers. This is a departure from that. BJORK: Lunacy is for people struggling, and letting them know that they’re not alone. So hopefully this work can also offer a space for those people to find belonging.

Let’s talk about perimenopause as a character in Lunacy . Is there any part of perimenopause that is exciting for you? BJORK: Oh lord, at this point? No. HAH! But what could feel exciting is the necessity of continuing to get to know yourself, especially now that I feel I have more understanding of what is going on, and also the letting go—and how this will change again…and again… and again. I don’t know what’s to come, or what else is to change or become off-kilter again, but I have seen the strength in myself to go on and keep trying to figure that out, and continuing to find help outside of myself for support—whether that is therapy, acupuncture, Western meds, or, importantly, my community.

I’ve heard people describe perimenopause as a time when raw feelings like rage become more unfiltered, maybe because we’re shedding expectations around nurturing and keeping the peace. Have you experienced some kind of shedding like that, and has it shaped your current imagery? BJORK: I have felt the shedding of another mask, of truly letting people know how I am feeling and what I am going through no matter how “ugly” society may deem that. Perimenopause is a part of our experience, one that 51 percent of the population will go through, and I think everyone should know more about that and be able to support those going through it. And I think we are at a point now where many of those people will be nonbinary/trans, and with that, those experiences should also be documented, supported, and understood.

You’ve said that you consider your work both documentation and manifestation. How does that manifestation work? BJORK: At times, drawing what I don’t understand or want to seek (i.e., spiritual growth), helps me move towards those things, and sometimes when the work is done I realize that I have done just that.

Something else you mention about this body of work is how it’s responding to the current hostility to queer communities. How has making work in a hostile climate changed you and what you chose to depict in your work? BJORK: What I depict in Lunacy feels like a departure from past themes—letting out more of my shadow self, the darker side, and being vulnerable in that way. Showing coping mechanisms to deal with the devastating reality we’re living in, regarding the hostility towards queer communities, and all minoritized communities, and being honest about the things I do to deal.

Is there anything you learned through making this show? BJORK: That I am able to continue to create what I want and that doesn’t have to be for anyone else, but hopefully it will offer something to others.
Does lunacy equal freedom? BJORK: I think yes, lunacy equals freedom, in a way of letting it all hang out there, being seen no matter what, and hopefully that leads to understanding.
Kelly Bjork: Lunacy is on view at J. Rinehart Gallery through Oct. 28, with an artist talk on Oct. 17.

articles.title: Free Will Astrology
articles.author: Rob Brezsny
paras: ARIES (March 21-April 19): In the practice of niwaki , Japanese gardeners shape trees so they look both natural and artfully composed. They prune and style the branches to dramatize the tree’s inherent character. Their goal is to collaborate. I recommend you experiment with a similar approach in the coming weeks, Aries. Try partnering with the living processes in your sphere rather than simply imposing your will on them. Ask yourself: What is trying to flourish here? Can I coax out some useful beauty? How can I coordinate my own intelligence with nature’s intelligence?

TAURUS (April 20-May 20): Your spirit creatures for the coming weeks are the slow-moving giant tortoises of the Galápagos Islands. They can live for more than a century. They conserve energy, move deliberately, and carry their protection with them. I believe you will benefit from embracing their ways in the coming weeks, Taurus. Refuse to be rushed or pressured, either by others or yourself. Proceed at the precise rate you need to. Your natural strength will thrive through your incremental steadiness. PS: Consider giving yourself a tortoise nickname.

GEMINI (May 21-June 20): A master perfumer composes a fragrance in three layers. The top notes are what you smell first. They’re vivid and volatile. The next layer blooms gradually, unfurling the heart notes of the fragrance. Underneath everything are the deep, resinous base notes, which don’t fully reveal themselves for hours and cling longest to the skin. Let this be a metaphor to guide your joys and pleasures in the coming weeks, Gemini. Relish the bright top notes that flare and vanish, but persist long enough for the heart to open, and longer still for the deep base notes to emerge. Gather all the rich delights, not just some.

CANCER (June 21-July 22): It’s hard, scary work for a crab to molt its shell and grow a bigger one. As it waits for its new protection to grow, its soft, tender body is exposed and vulnerable. That’s why it often hides in rock crevices, neither moving nor eating until its armor returns. Your situation, dear Cancerian, isn’t nearly as dire as the poor, defenseless crab’s. But as you power through your own personal molting season, I urge you to enhance your psychic protection. You need to feel extra safe and secure.

LEO (July 23-Aug. 22): Bats navigate by echolocation. They send out sounds and interpret the echoes. But when competing for food, they may also jam each other’s sonar, generating acoustic interference that makes navigation harder for rivals. A similar phenomenon occurs in human populations. Some of the noisy talk we hear is other people’s jamming signals. Consciously or unconsciously, they’re creating interference that may make it harder for us to navigate. Now is a good time for you to learn better how to distinguish between real information and meaningless hubbub. Refine your filters.

VIRGO (Aug. 23-Sept. 22): Jan Tschichold (1902–1974) was a brilliant typographer who revolutionized graphic design. He left his mark on millions of books. But later in life, he rejected some of his own rules, returning to classical typography and critiquing his earlier work as too rigid. In this spirit, dear Virgo, I will ask you if some of your long-standing rules no longer serve you. Is it possible that some of your own “best practices” may have calcified into unexamined dogma? The coming months will invite productive heresy against your past selves. You’re allowed to contradict your earlier convictions. Hint: Your vigorous evolution requires it.

LIBRA (Sept. 23-Oct. 22): In the 18th century, Libran philosopher Denis Diderot was instrumental in creating the Encyclopédie . It wasn’t the first compendium of the world’s knowledge, but it was the most ambitious and comprehensive. In 28 volumes, it assembled contributions from a large number of writers, including leading figures of the French Enlightenment. Robust collaboration was key to its enduring influence. In the coming weeks, Libra, I’m hoping that you, like Diderot, will be an initiator and facilitator of rich cooperation. Conversations, partnerships, and shared projects could generate insights that none of the participants would have discovered alone. By inviting multiple perspectives into the discussion, you will help cultivate a fertile weave of ideas.

SCORPIO (Oct. 23-Nov. 21): In the volcanic seas around Iceland, underwater eruptions sometimes build entirely new islands that rise from the waves as bare, black rock. During the ensuing years, wind and waves and seabirds seed them with life. Mosses, lichens, hardy plants, and nesting birds slowly transform the raw lava into a living shore. I’m rooting for you to instigate a similar process, Scorpio. My prediction: A development that initially seems stark or unfinished could become fertile ground for growth. Your perceptive instincts will recognize possibilities before they are obvious to others. Be patient with beginnings that look raw.

SAGITTARIUS (Nov. 22-Dec. 21): I invite you to achieve minor miracles that will enable you to brag at parties about how you created something out of nothing. Not in a loud, egotistical way, but with a sly glimmer in your eye, as if you’re sharing secrets about how reality can be coaxed into generosity if you approach it with imagination and chutzpah. Yes, dear Sagittarius, I’m ecstatic to inform you that now is a favorable moment to turn scraps into usefulness, boredom into invention, and vague hunches into tangible results. Be alert! Be on the lookout! Scout around for raw materials that have been overlooked or dismissed. Half-abandoned projects? Mercurial inclinations? Fugitive fantasies? Seemingly idle conversations that reveal marvelous glints and gleams? These are examples of the “nothings” you can turn into treasures.

CAPRICORN (Dec. 22-Jan. 19): I’ve got a rough, tough assignment for you: Dare yourself to be startled by your own exquisite beauty. Be bold and even brazen in appreciating what a marvelous creature you are. Can you summon the necessary audacity? I think you can. Please notice the ways you have underestimated your gifts, minimized your impact, or edited out your brilliance to make others comfortable. Allow yourself to feel the tender shock of recognizing that you’re more interesting and mysteriously compelling than you’ve been trained to believe. PS: This will help you call on even deeper inner resources in the coming weeks.

AQUARIUS (Jan. 20-Feb. 18): Aquarian writer Virginia Woolf was a fount of interesting ideas. Sometimes she pushed her active mind to track them down and capture them, but on other occasions, she enjoyed gathering gems that arrived as her imagination wandered and drifted. These “moments of being” provided her with small treasures while she was walking in nature, taking a bath, or doing nothing in particular. I believe that you are now primed to experience many such pleasurable eruptions of insight. In the coming weeks, pauses and lulls and intermissions will open unexpected portals.

PISCES (Feb. 19-March 20): For the low price of $199, I could expertly dispel that annoying curse you’ve been lugging around. But I would feel sleazy taking your cash when you are fully capable of zapping the curse yourself. So instead I will recommend that you perform the banishing ritual, then write yourself a check for $199. Here’s how. Step 1: Visualize an object that represents the curse. Imagine hurling it into a beach bonfire and watching it burn. Step 2: Bring to mind a person you believe contributes to the curse. Envision a rope that ties the two of you together, waist to waist. articles.title: Wilson Delivers New Gun Violence Prevention Plan
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: Last week, Mayor Katie Wilson introduced a plan to reduce gun violence in Seattle that is designed to improve coordination between departments and agencies while implementing the strategy of focused deterrence that has been successful in reducing gun violence in several other American cities.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!
Having been in development since Wilson took office less than nine months ago, the plan takes its cues from last year’s Seattle Office of the City Auditor’s recommendations .

Notably, all of Seattle’s community violence intervention (CVI) work will be moved to the Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) Department, a move that was recommended by the auditor’s office last year and was envisioned as one of the roles CARE would fulfill in the City Charter. Two new positions have been created – a Director and Coordinator of Gun Violence Reduction – to oversee the implementation of Wilson’s plan within CARE.

“The plan’s purpose is to fix the lack of coordination that has limited our impact and to put new programs in place that strengthen our response to ending gun violence,” Alex Hudson, a spokesperson for the Mayor’s Office, told The Urbanist . “Our city hasn’t ever in its history dedicated staff outside of law enforcement to shooting response. Placing this coordination in the same department as 9-1-1, with immediate access to real-time shooting information, is a huge step for our City’s ability to respond to gun violence events with both intervention and accountability.”

Through the 2027 budget, $5 million of Community Violence Intervention (CVI) contracts with nine organizations will be transferred from the Human Services Department (HSD) to CARE. This move will more closely link the City’s CVI work to the Seattle Police Department (SPD), which has been developing its own Community Violence Task Force in order to begin implementation of a focused deterrence strategy to reduce gun violence.

“Moving CVI contracts to CARE will facilitate tighter coordination with SPD and enable Chief Barden’s and Sayles’ teams to identify, track, and coordinate information sharing about accountability metrics for the service providers,” Hudson said. “Moving the work into CARE will also avail 9-1-1 dispatchers and first responders of more information about who is under case management or has an active safety plan in place. This represents an important shift toward a coordinated care environment that supports safe and effective service delivery.”

The City will be collaborating with the University of Washington's Center for Firearm Injury Prevention to perform a citywide mapping of related programs and data, otherwise known as a landscape analysis. Hudson said this process is expected to take three to six months and is starting immediately.

Finally, with help from Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, the City will be beginning its first Violence Reduction Council (VRC), a public health model that brings together public health, social service agencies, and criminal legal system partners to review every homicide in order to identify systemic improvements. The auditor’s report last year said that Johns Hopkins researchers had offered free technical assistance to implement this framework.

In addition, more than $8 million will be invested through HSD in programs to prevent violence through support to young people and their families. At the same time, SPD will be increasing bicycle patrols in Belltown, North Aurora Ave N, Little Saigon, and Rainier Beach and better coordinate its Narcotics Unit operations with its Community Response Group and Gun Violence Reduction Unit.

Wilson’s plan has received sharp criticism from certain councilmembers, particularly from Councilmember Maritza Rivera, who introduced a competing plan via a non-binding resolution that passed last Tuesday, with two councilmembers – Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Dionne Foster – abstaining.

Rivera’s plan consists of hiring consulting services from the National Network of Safe Communities (NNSC), a research center at the John Jay College of Criminal Justice. The consulting contract would cost the City $417,000 over two years.

“There is no downside to bringing the National Network for Safe Communities here and to implement this strategy with fidelity, in the hopes that we too will see the same results in gun violence reductions that these other cities have seen,” Rivera said at the full council meeting last week. “The only downside is not acting.”

The audit with recommendations on how the City could improve its gun violence prevention efforts was released last March during Mayor Bruce Harrell’s administration, but it wasn’t until Wilson took office this year that Rivera sprung into action. In June, she held a symposium on the topic and introduced her own resolution shortly thereafter.

At the meeting last Tuesday, Rivera objected to Wilson’s gun violence prevention plan, saying that it doesn’t focus on the focused deterrence strategy that the founder of the NNSC had initially developed.
“[The Mayor’s Office is] not interested in doing actual focused deterrence because it involves police. I mean, that's just the bottom line,” Rivera said.

CARE Chief Amy Barden, who will now be overseeing the City’s gun violence prevention work, has been studying the best evidence-based strategy since her arrival at CARE, and disagreed with this characterization.

“I don't think people understand that SPD developed a very effective Community Violence Task Force in 2023 (the same time the CARE ordinance was articulated), using world class research methodology under the leadership of Cambridge-educated PhD Loren Atherley, which explains the precipitous drop in local gun violence outpacing the national trend since 2023,” Barden told The Urbanist .

“However, the [task force] was half of the equation,” Barden continued. “The focused deterrence model centers community-based supports and interventions, and we never connected those services to the accountability component in SPD. The CVI contracts housed in HSD were not coordinated with the larger strategy, and that is the significance of the Mayor's proposal.”
Barden is eager to begin the work outlined in the new violence prevention plan.
“It would be a dereliction of duty to not move as quickly as possible to save lives; it is our young people who are most vulnerable to gun violence in Seattle,” Barden said.
The Mayor’s Office also stated their support for a focused deterrence strategy but thinks they can implement the strategy without spending the money on the NNSC contract.

“Focused deterrence is a core component of the Mayor’s plan, and SPD is already laying the groundwork for this work,” Hudson said. “Focused deterrence is an academic theory and strategy not owned by any one organization, implemented in different ways by different cities, and studied extensively.”

Baltimore, the American city most often held up as an example of the success of focused deterrence, saw a significant drop in shootings and homicides within 18 months of their latest attempt at the strategy. Long a city with a high murder rate, Baltimore recorded 133 homicides in 2025, its lowest homicide total and rate in nearly 50 years. That historic year still put the Charm City at five times the homicide rate of Seattle, which tallied 37 homicides in 2025, even with a population that is about 250,000 residents greater.

Despite its recent success, the City of Baltimore had two previous attempts that weren’t as effective. During the second attempt, The Trace reported that the City didn’t follow through on the promised services to the program’s participants. The NNSC was the consultant on Baltimore’s first two unsuccessful attempts, but not on its heralded third try that did appear to break through, as PubliCola ’s Erica Barnett noted .

“It took several tries for Baltimore to get it quite right, and I believe on the third try they might have had multiple consultants,” Councilmember Eddie Lin said during the council discussion of Rivera’s proposal. “And so for me, it's less about a particular consultant.”
Lin, who voted in favor of the resolution, said he saw it as a first step.
Councilmember Debora Juarez spoke directly against Wilson’s plan.
“This is not a plan,” Juarez said. “It's a picture, a window, if you will, a rearview window. It's not forward-looking. There's no vision, and we're already doing these things.”

There are several components to Wilson’s plan that are already in place, including existing investments in resources for youth and the new attorney in the Seattle City Attorney’s Office charged with filing Extreme Risk Protection Orders to try to prevent gun access to high-risk individuals that was announced in June .

However, the improved coordination provided by moving the violence intervention work and contracts into CARE, the two new leadership positions for gun violence prevention efforts within CARE, the work with the University of Washington to prepare a landscape analysis, and setting up a Violence Reduction Council are all new. Wilson’s plan also includes funds to start a new pilot afterschool program at Rainier Beach High School and a new Teen Late Night pilot at High Point Community Center, as well as hiring two new HSD employees to better coordinate Seattle’s Community Safety Network for school-related violence interruption work.

Juarez also objected to partnering with the University of Washington, saying that “sometimes I think when people are too local, they're too political, and they're too close to it to actually give us a solid and somber assessment of what we need to do.”
Quibbles aside, UW’s Center for Firearm Injury Prevention is one of the top research centers on the topic in the nation.
Beyond the dustup over focused deterrence, the mayor’s plan includes a few other elements that are likely to face scrutiny.

Harrell oversaw a deal between the Department of Education and Early Learning (DEEL) and the online mental health provider Talkspace at the end of 2024. The City signed a contract with Talkspace to provide virtual mental health services to Seattle’s students in the wake of a decision by City Council to make a slight increase in the JumpStart tax in order to provide funding for students to have more mental health support.

In early 2025, reporting by Gizmodo uncovered online tracking pixels on Talkspace’s web pages for teen mental health services for the cities of New York City, Baltimore, and Seattle. The trackers sent information about who was visiting the Talkspace site to an array of social media firms such as TikTok, Meta, SnapChat, and Google. DEEL was not aware of this issue until Gizmodo ’s reporting.

Earlier this year, when The Urbanist asked DEEL why the contract with TalkSpace was continued after this discovery, a spokesperson for the department said, “DEEL continued our contract with TalkSpace because they addressed our data privacy concerns. Additionally, youth were actively using the service and we did not want to disrupt their care.”
However, data privacy experts say there are still concerns around using the service.

In addition, recent reporting in The Seattle Times found that the Talkspace service has been vastly underutilized compared to its cost, with only 442 students being provided therapy when the expected number had been 2,200 to 4,400, an issue of which City officials were aware.
A new contract with Talkspace was signed this summer.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Quiet Zone in Kent
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On August 24, 2026, Kent’s long-awaited Quiet Zone took effect along the BNSF Railway mainline through downtown. This designation, granted by the Federal Railroad Administration in June , no longer requires trains to sound their horn when approaching an at-grade crossing. Over the past 14 years, the City of Kent has worked to meet the necessary requirements to achieve a Quiet Zone. Recent infrastructure upgrades include building raised concrete medians, adding additional signs, and refreshing pavement markings. In a non-Quiet Zone area, all trains are required to sound their horn 15-20 seconds before each street crossing.

The BNSF mainline tracks are used by 38 passenger trains and many more freight trains every day. The frequent at-grade crossings in downtown Kent resulted in nearby residents hearing hundreds of train horns day and night. The Quiet Zone stretches between S 212th St and S 259th St. The following crossings are included:

As safety is still a top priority, train engineers are still allowed to sound the horn in emergency situations or as they deem necessary. While the Quiet Zone is officially in effect, it may take some time for nearby residents to hear a difference. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.
